fetched_contents.text: Basic Information about Landfill Gas Landfill gas (LFG) is a natural byproduct of the decomposition of organic material in landfills. LFG is composed of roughly 50 percent methane (the primary component of natural gas), 50 percent carbon dioxide (CO2) and a small amount of non-methane organic compounds. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas at least 28 times more effective than CO2 at trapping heat in the atmosphere over a 100-year period, per the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assessment report (AR5). Learn more about methane emissions in the United States. On this page: * Methane Emissions from Landfills * Collecting and Treating Landfill Gas * Landfill Gas Energy Project Types ---------------------------------------- Methane Emissions from Landfills Municipal solid waste (MSW) landfills are the third-largest source of human-related methane emissions in the United States, accounting for approximately 14.4 percent of these emissions in 2022. The methane emissions from MSW landfills in 2022 were approximately equivalent to the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from more than 24.0 million gasoline-powered passenger vehicles driven for one year or the CO2 emissions from more than 13.1 million homes’ energy use for one year. At the same time, methane emissions from MSW landfills represent a lost opportunity to capture and use a significant energy resource. When MSW is first deposited in a landfill, it undergoes an aerobic (with oxygen) decomposition stage when little methane is generated. Then, typically within less than 1 year, anaerobic conditions are established and methane-producing bacteria begin to decompose the waste and generate methane. Learn about alternative options for managing organic waste. The following diagram illustrates the changes in typical LFG composition after waste placement. Bacteria decompose landfill waste in four phases. Gas composition changes with each phase and waste in a landfill may be undergoing several phases of decomposition at once. The time after placement scale (total time and phase duration) varies with landfill conditions. Figure adapted from ATSDR 2008. Chapter 2: Landfill Gas Basics. In Landfill Gas Primer - An Overview for Environmental Health Professionals. Figure 2-1, pp. 5-6. https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/HAC/landfill/PDFs/Landfill_2001_ch2mod.pdf (PDF)(12 pp, 2MB) Learn more in Chapter 1. Landfill Gas Energy Basics of LMOP's LFG Energy Project Development Handbook. In October 2009, EPA issued a rule (40 CFR Part 98) that requires the reporting of (GHG) emissions from large sources and suppliers in the United States, and is intended to collect accurate and timely emissions data to inform future policy decisions. * Learn more about EPA's Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program * Learn more about GHG emissions from the waste sector Annually, EPA issues an inventory report to present the U.S. government's estimates of U.S. human-related GHG emissions and sinks for each year since 1990. Emissions from the waste sector as well as other sectors are presented in this inventory. * Review EPA's Inventory of U.S. Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks Collecting and Treating Landfill Gas Instead of escaping into the air, LFG can be captured, converted, and used as a renewable energy resource. Using LFG helps to reduce odors and other hazards associated with LFG emissions, and prevents methane from migrating into the atmosphere and contributing to local smog and global climate change. In addition, LFG energy projects generate revenue and create jobs in the community and beyond. Learn more about the benefits of using LFG. Flowchart of a Basic LFG Collection and Processing System LFG is extracted from landfills using a series of wells and a blower/flare (or vacuum) system. This system directs the collected gas to a central point where it can be processed and treated depending upon the ultimate use for the gas. From this point, the gas can be flared or beneficially used in an LFG energy project. Click on the flowchart to view more details, including photographs of LFG collection and processing systems. — Click on the flowchart to view details — Landfill Gas Energy Project Types There are many options available for converting LFG into energy. Different types of LFG energy projects are grouped below into three broad categories – Electricity Generation, Direct Use of Medium-Btu Gas, and Renewable Natural Gas. Descriptions of project technologies are included under each project type. For more information on LFG energy project technology options and the advantages and disadvantages of each, see Chapter 3. Project Technology Options of LMOP’s LFG Energy Project Development Handbook. Owners of LFG electricity projects may benefit from reviewing LMOP’s Toolkit for Expiring LFG Electricity Power Purchase Agreements to help them evaluate options for either continuing to generate electricity or to switch to another project type. Electricity Generation About 63 percent of currently operational LFG energy projects in the United States generate electricity. A variety of technologies, including reciprocating internal combustion engines, turbines, microturbines and fuel cells, can be used to generate electricity for onsite use and/or sale to the grid. The reciprocating engine is the most commonly used conversion technology for LFG electricity applications because of its relatively low cost, high efficiency and size ranges that complement the gas output of many landfills. Gas turbines are typically used in larger LFG energy projects while microturbines are generally used for smaller LFG volumes and in niche applications. Cogeneration, also known as combined heat and power (CHP), projects use LFG to generate both electricity and thermal energy, usually in the form of steam or hot water. Landfilling plastics severely limits resource recovery and recyclability because it removes high-value materials from the waste stream before they can be sorted, processed, and reintegrated into the economy. The evidence shows that landfilling prevents material recovery by diverting recyclable plastics away from recovery infrastructure, effectively reducing the supply of market-ready recyclables. For example, EPA’s facts and figures indicate that in 2018, only about 32.1% of municipal solid waste was recycled or composted, leaving a large portion of recyclable materials landfilled or otherwise disposed of [N2-F3]. A separate source on plastics recycling notes that the U.S. national recycling rate was 36% in 2018, reinforcing the idea that a significant share of plastics remains outside the recovery system [N2-R2]. This means landfilling not only wastes the material itself but also reduces the availability of high-quality recyclables needed for downstream processing.

The loss of recyclable plastics from the waste stream has direct effects on downstream recovery infrastructure and economics. When plastics are landfilled, they become unavailable for mechanical or chemical recycling, and the residual waste stream is less valuable for recovery operations. The search evidence on plastics recycling also emphasizes that recycling is economically and environmentally sensible, implying that landfilling undermines both the economic viability and environmental benefit of recovery [N2-R5]. Furthermore, the “Paths to circularity for plastics in the United States” source says that scaling up existing commercial recycling could divert up to 68% of plastic waste from landfills, underscoring how landfilling limits the scale and effectiveness of recovery systems [N2-R3].

In comparing landfilling with recycling pathways, the evidence suggests that landfilling is structurally less compatible with resource recovery than mechanical or chemical recycling. Mechanical recycling relies on clean, intact materials, while chemical recycling can process lower-quality or contaminated feedstock, but both depend on access to the waste stream. Landfilling prevents this access and can degrade plastics beyond recoverability, reducing the quality and quantity of available feedstock for recycling. The comparison source on waste-to-energy versus landfill also frames landfilling as a last-resort option with higher environmental costs than recycling, reinforcing the idea that landfilling is an inefficient recovery strategy relative to more circular alternatives [N4-R2]. While the provided evidence does not explicitly detail chemical versus mechanical pathways in depth, it does establish that landfilling is a major barrier to recovery and that recycling and energy recovery generally have lower environmental impacts than landfilling [N4-R3].

Overall, landfilling plastics reduces material recovery by removing plastics from the waste stream, diminishes the availability of high-quality recyclables, weakens downstream recovery infrastructure, and limits the economic and environmental value of plastics through premature disposal. The evidence supports a clear conclusion: landfilling is not a resource recovery solution and instead creates a loss of recoverable value [N2-F3][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-R2][N4-R3].

Landfilling plastics has significant land use and spatial consequences, including land consumption, conflicts with competing land uses, siting challenges, and long-term land degradation. The evidence points to landfill footprint and land surface design as important spatial considerations, with studies examining landfill geometrical shape, compactness, and land surface design [N3-R1]. It also notes that landfilling can occupy large land areas and generate substantial impacts on land use, consistent with the idea that landfill sites require substantial land consumption [N3-R3]. The landfill footprint literature suggests that landfill design and siting are not trivial; landfill shape and geometry influence land use efficiency and environmental performance [N3-R1][N3-R3].

Conflicts with urban, agricultural, or ecological land uses are a major concern. The evidence from landfill footprint studies implies that landfilling can compete with other land uses because it occupies land that could otherwise support urban development, agriculture, or ecological functions [N3-R3]. This is especially relevant because landfill siting is constrained by topography, soils, hydrologic conditions, and flood protection requirements, which themselves affect spatial planning [N5-F2]. The TSCA landfill inspection guidance manual emphasizes siting considerations such as soils, hydrologic conditions, flood protection, and topography, showing that landfill placement is a complex planning task that must balance environmental and spatial constraints [N5-F2]. This means landfilling can create spatial conflicts by requiring land to be set aside for waste disposal rather than for more productive or ecologically valuable uses.

Spatial planning and siting challenges are directly supported by the evidence. Landfill siting must account for soil and hydrologic conditions, flood protection, and topography, all of which affect where a landfill can be placed and how it is designed [N5-F2]. The landfill footprint study also highlights that landfill design and shape matter for land use efficiency, suggesting that siting is not only about location but also about optimizing the footprint and minimizing land consumption [N3-R1]. These siting constraints imply that landfilling is inherently spatially demanding and that good planning is required to avoid environmental and social conflicts.

Long-term land degradation and site reuse limitations are also evident in the evidence. Landfills can degrade land over time, and the TSCA guidance manual notes that landfill operations must manage leachate, groundwater contamination, and site integrity to prevent long-term environmental damage [N5-F2]. The landfill footprint literature also implies that landfills are long-lived and that their design and management affect how land can be reused after closure [N3-R1]. Together, these sources suggest that landfilling does not simply occupy land; it degrades land and often limits its reuse, creating lasting spatial and environmental costs [N5-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].

In summary, landfilling plastics consumes land, creates spatial conflicts with competing land uses, complicates siting and planning, and can lead to long-term land degradation and site reuse limitations [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F2].

The EPA landfill gas page explains that landfill gas is composed largely of methane, which is a potent greenhouse gas at least 28 times more effective than CO2 at trapping heat over a 100-year period [N1-F1]. It also states that MSW landfills are the third-largest source of human-related methane emissions in the United States, accounting for about 14.4% of these emissions in 2022 [N1-F1]. The evidence further notes that methane emissions from landfills represent a lost opportunity to capture and use energy, and that they contribute to local smog and global climate change [N1-F1]. This establishes landfilling as a major climate problem, not only through direct emissions but also through the loss of energy recovery potential.

The EPA landfill gas page explicitly states that landfill gas can be collected and treated to reduce odors and other hazards associated with emissions, indicating that landfilling can produce harmful air quality impacts [N1-F1]. The landfill inspection guidance manual also emphasizes that landfill operations must manage leachate and groundwater contamination, which are linked to broader environmental and toxic risks [N5-F2]. Although the evidence does not provide detailed toxic pollutant lists, it clearly frames landfilling as a source of environmental hazards that require technical controls to mitigate air and water pollution [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Landfilling also leads to microplastic and chemical leachate formation in landfills. The loss of economic and environmental value from degraded plastics is another important consequence. The recovery implications of plastic type and composition are significant. This means that some plastics may be more likely to persist, degrade, or leach pollutants than others, making recovery and management more difficult [N5-R3][N5-F2].

The comparison evidence on waste-to-energy versus landfill frames landfilling as a last-resort option with higher environmental costs than recycling [N4-R2]. While the provided evidence does not explicitly detail chemical versus mechanical pathways in depth, it does establish that landfilling is a major barrier to recovery and that recycling and energy recovery generally have lower environmental impacts than landfilling [N4-R3]. In practical terms, this means landfilling raises the cost and complexity of recovery operations while reducing the economic value of recyclable plastics.

### D) Comparison with mechanical and chemical recycling pathways
Landfilling is structurally less compatible with resource recovery than mechanical or chemical recycling. Mechanical recycling relies on clean, intact materials, while chemical recycling can process lower-quality or contaminated feedstock, but both depend on access to the waste stream. Landfilling prevents this access and can degrade plastics beyond recoverability, reducing the quality and quantity of available feedstock for recycling [N8]. The evidence supports the broader conclusion that landfilling is not a resource recovery solution and instead creates a loss of recoverable value [N2-F3][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-R2][N4-R3].

## 3) Land use and spatial consequences of landfilling plastics

### A) Land consumption and land use footprint of landfill sites
Landfilling plastics consumes land and has a substantial land use footprint. The evidence points to landfill footprint and land surface design as important spatial considerations, with studies examining landfill geometrical shape, compactness, and land surface design [N9]. It also notes that landfilling can occupy large land areas and generate substantial impacts on land use [N3-R3]. The landfill footprint literature suggests that landfill design and siting are not trivial; landfill shape and geometry influence land use efficiency and environmental performance [N3-R1][N3-R3].

### B) Conflicts with urban, agricultural, or ecological land uses
Landfilling creates conflicts with competing land uses because it occupies land that could otherwise support urban development, agriculture, or ecological functions [N9]. The evidence on landfill siting emphasizes that landfill placement must account for soils, hydrologic conditions, flood protection, and topography, which are spatial planning constraints [N5-F2]. This means landfilling can create spatial conflicts by requiring land to be set aside for waste disposal rather than for more productive or ecologically valuable uses.

### C) Spatial planning and siting challenges
Spatial planning and siting challenges are a major consequence of landfilling. Landfill siting must balance environmental and spatial constraints, including soil and hydrologic conditions, flood protection, and topography [N5-F2]. The landfill footprint study also highlights that landfill design and shape matter for land use efficiency, suggesting that siting is not only about location but also about optimizing the footprint and minimizing land consumption [N3-R1]. These siting constraints imply that landfilling is inherently spatially demanding and that good planning is required to avoid environmental and social conflicts.

### D) Long-term land degradation and site reuse limitations
Landfilling can also lead to long-term land degradation and limit site reuse. The landfill inspection guidance manual notes that landfill operations must manage leachate, groundwater contamination, and site integrity to prevent long-term environmental damage [N5-F2]. The landfill footprint literature implies that landfills are long-lived and that their design and management affect how land can be reused after closure [N3-R1]. Together, these sources suggest that landfilling does not simply occupy land; it degrades land and often limits its reuse, creating lasting spatial and environmental costs [N5-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].

## 4) Plastic-specific recovery and degradation losses

### A) Reduction in the availability of high-quality recyclables
Landfilling plastics reduces the availability of high-quality recyclables because it removes plastics from the waste stream before they can be sorted and processed [N10]. The evidence on plastics recycling shows that in 2018 the U.S. national recycling rate was 36%, and that only about 32.1% of municipal solid waste was recycled or composted, leaving a large amount of recyclable material landfilled or otherwise disposed of [N2-R2][N2-F3]. This implies that landfilling plastics directly limits the supply of market-ready recyclables, which are essential for downstream recovery. The “Paths to circularity for plastics in the United States” source reinforces this by stating that scaling up existing commercial recycling could divert up to 68% of plastic waste from landfills, underscoring how landfilling diminishes the availability of recyclable materials [N2-R3].

### B) Microplastic and chemical leachate formation in landfills
Landfilling also leads to microplastic and chemical leachate formation in landfills. The plastic-specific degradation evidence indicates that landfill leachate can contain microplastics, and that microplastics in raw landfill leachate are largely attributable to local plastic waste production and solid waste management practices [N6-R3]. A separate source on microplastics in landfill leachate states that treated leachate samples had lower microplastic counts than untreated samples, showing that landfilling can generate microplastic contamination and that treatment can reduce it [N6-R4]. The landfill leachate management overview also notes that landfill leachate is a serious environmental problem and that older, unrestricted contaminant release landfills can lack controls on leachate and environmental contamination [N5-R3]. This means landfilling not only degrades plastics physically but also generates chemical leachate and microplastic pollutants that can escape into the environment [N5-R3][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### C) Loss of economic and environmental value from degraded plastics
The loss of economic and environmental value from degraded plastics is another important consequence. When plastics are landfilled, they are no longer available for recovery, and their degradation reduces their potential value. The evidence on plastics recycling emphasizes that recycling is economically and environmentally sensible, implying that landfilling undermines both the economic value and environmental benefit of plastics [N2-R5]. The landfill gas page also notes that methane emissions from landfills represent a lost opportunity to capture and use a significant energy resource, showing that landfilling can waste both material and energy value [N1-F1]. Landfilling therefore erodes the economic and environmental value of plastics by converting them into disposal costs rather than recovery opportunities.

### D) Recovery implications of plastic type and composition
The recovery implications of plastic type and composition are significant. The evidence on plastic waste degradation in landfill conditions explains that leachate characteristics depend on the specific types of waste, which means that different plastics may behave differently in landfills [N5-R3]. The landfill inspection guidance manual also notes that landfill leachate is unique and determined by the specific types of waste(s), reinforcing that plastic composition affects leachate generation and environmental impact [N5-F2]. This means that some plastics may be more likely to persist, degrade, or leach pollutants than others, making recovery and management more difficult [N5-R3][N5-F2].

---

## 5) Bottom line

In short, landfilling plastics is a triple burden: it harms the environment through leachate, methane, toxic pollutants, and long-term persistence; it weakens resource recovery by removing high-value recyclables from the waste stream and increasing the cost and complexity of downstream recovery; and it consumes land, creates spatial conflicts, and can degrade land over time. Plastic-specific losses further show that landfilling generates microplastics and chemical leachate, and that the recovery consequences depend on plastic type and composition [N7][N8][N9][N10].

If the goal is to reduce environmental harm and improve resource efficiency, landfilling plastics is not the solution. The evidence supports a transition toward better recovery, reuse, and alternative waste management options that preserve value rather than destroy it [N2-R3][N4-R3].
